title: Intensive Agriculture and Erosion Affect Composition of Soil Organic Matter
content:
Intensive agriculture drives SOC loss by raising erosion and altering organic matter fraction stoichiometry. Cultivation and erosion decreased the C/N ratios of POM, MAOM, and DOM but increased the contribution of microbial residues to MAOM, shifting MAOM formation from POM-dominated toward increased microbial and DOM inputs.


ABSTRACT

Land-use changes induced by human activities usually accelerate soil erosion, leading to losses of soil organic matter (SOM). The mechanisms by which cultivation-associated degradation affects SOM composition via changes of content and quality of particulate (POM), mineral-associated (MAOM), dissolved organic matter (DOM), and microbial biomass are not elucidated. We investigated the C:N stoichiometry of these fractions, and erosion (using 137Cs activity) along a chronosequence of cultivation-associated degradation (0–114 years) in Mollisols. Two-pool and Bayesian three-source mixing models estimated contributions of microbial biomass, DOM, and POM to MAOM to the total SOM. Erosion intensity ranged locally from 440 to 4800 t km−2 year−1, resulting in cumulative soil losses of 11,000 to 320,000 t km−2 over 114 years of cultivation. As cultivation duration and eroded amounts increased, the C/N ratios of POM, MAOM, and DOM declined owing to (i) the faster loss of C than N, (ii) a decrease in C/N with soil depth involved in tillage horizon, and (iii) N input by fertilization. These higher C than N losses reflect that erosion is not the sole process leading to the decline of C stocks, but intensive cultivation also accelerates organic matter mineralization and CO2 release to the atmosphere. As the C/N ratios of POM and MAOM declined but microbial C/N increased, the estimated contribution of microbial inputs to MAOM increased from 6% to 32%. The Bayesian model partitioned MAOM sources into DOM (8%), microbial (11%), and POM (81%), reinforcing that POM dominates MAOM formation in croplands. Cultivation-associated degradation led to SOC losses by reducing POM-C/N and MAOM-C/N ratios, while erosion strongly accelerated these effects. Furthermore, cultivation-associated degradation is also based on the limited inputs of organic C as the precursors for MAOM formation by depleting POM. These results from a > 100-year chronosequence indicate that cultivation-induced degradation reduces SOM content, while also shifting the MAOM composition progressively towards a greater contribution of microbial C.
